name: Lactic acid
lead: Lactic acid (C3H6O3) is an alpha hydroxy acid (AHA) that occurs in sour milk and fermented foods and is produced in animal tissue as lactate during normal metabolism and exercise [1]. In skin care it is used as an exfoliant: in toners, serums, lotions and professional peels it loosens the bonds between dead cells on the skin surface so they shed, which people use to smooth rough texture, brighten a dull complexion and even out tone. Wikipedia notes its use in topical preparations and cosmetics for pH adjustment, disinfectant and keratolytic (skin-softening) properties [1]. Salts such as ammonium lactate are used in moisturizers for dry skin [2][3].

Among the common AHAs, lactic acid has a somewhat larger molecule than glycolic acid, and it is one of the acids that appears in the mildest tier of chemical peels, alongside glycolic acid [20]. It has been studied for hyperpigmentation, including an open trial of an 82 percent peel in melasma, and AHAs in general are widely used in anti-aging and texture-improving products [4][5]. A 2018 narrative review describes AHA effects as depending strongly on concentration, with high-strength peeling products behaving differently from low-strength ones [5].

Several other things share the name. Lactic acid bacteria are used in fermented foods and probiotics, poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) is an injectable collagen-stimulating filler marketed as Sculptra, and the muscle metabolite lactate features in exercise physiology. These are chemically related but are separate subjects from topical lactic acid [1][6][7][22].

chain: Lactic acid is applied to the skin as a toner, serum, lotion or peel
It loosens bonds between dead surface cells so they shed
Smoother-feeling, brighter-looking skin with a more even tone
angle.text: People use lactic acid products to exfoliate rough, dull or uneven skin, either as regular leave-on products or as periodic professional peels. The visible aim is smoother texture and a brighter, more even complexion; lactate salts in lotions are used for dry, flaky skin.

paras: Lactic acid appears in exfoliating toners and serums, body lotions and chemical peels intended to improve rough texture, dullness and uneven tone [5]. Wikipedia's chemical peel article places AHA peels (glycolic and lactic acid) in the mildest category, used for fine lines, dryness, uneven pigmentation and acne, and notes that lower-strength versions are common in home products; professional peels are usually performed by dermatologists or licensed estheticians [20].

Lactic acid is also a component of the skin's own natural moisturizing complex, according to a 2018 review, which cites earlier work finding it less irritating than glycolic acid [5]. Ammonium lactate, a salt of lactic acid, is the active ingredient in moisturizing lotions that have been tested in dry skin [2][3].

A 2014 study tested a high-concentration (82 percent) lactic acid preparation for melasma, a patchy facial pigmentation [4]. Wikipedia's skin-care article adds that chemical exfoliants are generally regarded as less harsh than mechanical scrubs, while cautioning that excessive exfoliation can irritate the skin and damage its barrier [23].

Industrially lactic acid is a food acidulant and preservative approved in the EU, US and Australia and New Zealand, and the monomer for polylactic acid bioplastics [1]. Wikipedia reports lactate was the 289th most commonly prescribed medication in the United States in 2023, a figure that reflects lactate-containing fluids such as lactated Ringer's solution [1]. A DailyMed entry lists an oral homeopathic-style product labelled for muscular overexertion pain [8].

A 2018 review in Molecules describes the basic AHA mechanism: AHAs reduce the cohesion between corneocytes (the flattened dead cells of the outer skin) above the granular layer, which drives desquamation, partly through lowered pH disrupting the protein junctions that hold the cells together [5]. Cited work in the review reports that AHAs can also thicken skin and increase glycosaminoglycans, and that a 20 percent citric acid preparation increased epidermal thickness in sun-damaged skin [5].

The same review frames the effect as concentration dependent. In its account, high concentrations act as peeling agents that can irritate and increase UV damage, while low concentrations may be protective; for lactic acid specifically, lab experiments in cultured keratinocytes at millimolar concentrations produced cell-cycle arrest and cell death, and the review calls the UVB findings phototoxic while noting that some supporting data are labelled as not shown [5]. The review also lists its own limits: it is a narrative rather than systematic review that leans on the authors' own studies [5].

Chemical peels remove the outermost layers of skin through controlled injury, after which the skin sheds. Wikipedia lists the types from lightest to deepest as AHA peels, beta hydroxy acid (salicylic acid) peels, retinoic acid peels, trichloroacetic acid medium peels and phenol-croton oil deep peels, and says the deeper the peel, the more complications can arise [20]. Light peels usually need no anaesthetic, with patients feeling mild stinging [20]. The practice dates to the second half of the 19th century, when the Austrian dermatologist Ferdinand Ritter von Hebra used agents such as phenol, croton oil and nitric acid [20].

In the 2014 melasma trial of an 82 percent lactic acid peel, participants had Fitzpatrick skin types IV and V, and the study excluded pregnant or lactating women, people taking oral contraceptives and those with recent facial procedures or photosensitizing drugs [4].

Published evidence for topical lactic acid consists mostly of small studies. In the 2014 melasma study, mean MASI (a melasma severity score) fell from 2.885 at baseline to 1.865 at week 12, about a 35 percent improvement, and stayed near that level at weeks 20 and 24 [4]. The share of patients graded as mildest severity rose from 25 percent to 80 percent by week 12 [4]. The study had no comparison group [4].

A registered phase 3 study compared 12 percent ammonium lactate with 10 percent urea cream in older adults with xerosis (dry skin), and an industry-sponsored study examined an AmLactin lotion with ceramides in 56 women with dry skin for moisturization and desquamation [2][3].

Common reactions to AHA products are redness, swelling, burning and itching; peels can also lead to post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, infection, scarring, allergic reactions and milia, according to the 2018 review, which names concentration, pH, exposure time and free acid content as risk factors [5]. In the 2014 melasma trial, burning was the only side effect reported [4].

Wikipedia reports that the US FDA and the Cosmetic Ingredient Review expert panels consider AHAs safe at low concentrations, at a pH above 3.5, with safety instructions, and advise sun-exposure care while using them; an industry-sponsored study linked AHAs to greater likelihood of sunburn, an effect described as reversible once use stops [19]. A 1999 randomized comparative trial in Acta Dermato-Venereologica examined stinging in rosacea [10].

Concentrated lactic acid carries a corrosive hazard classification (skin irritation and serious eye damage) on safety labelling [1]. A series of registered safety and compatibility studies of lactic acid-based intimate hygiene washes in Brazil (Dermacyd and Lactacyd products) enrolled between 27 and 559 participants [11][12][13].
Applied topically, lactic acid is described as a keratolytic that promotes exfoliation [1][5].

In the body, L-lactate is produced from pyruvate by lactate dehydrogenase. It is the primary endogenous agonist of the HCA1 receptor, which inhibits lipolysis in fat cells, and it serves as an energy substrate for neurons and as a pH buffer in exercising muscle [1]. Blood lactate above roughly 2.0 to 2.5 mmol/L is considered elevated, and lactic acidosis is defined by a blood pH below 7.35 [1].

Lactic acid is an alpha hydroxy acid with its hydroxyl group next to the carboxyl group. It is chiral, with L- and D-enantiomers and a 1:1 racemic mixture; the pKa is 3.86 and it is miscible with water [1]. The 2018 review reports that L(+) and synthetic DL forms were described as equally effective for increasing cell renewal [5]. It is made mainly by bacterial fermentation of carbohydrates, which can yield up to 99.9 percent L-lactic acid, and also by chemical synthesis from acetaldehyde via lactonitrile [1]. Two molecules can dehydrate to lactide, which polymerizes to polylactide [1].
Glycolic acid, the other widely used cosmetic AHA, has the formula C2H4O3 and a molar mass of about 76 g/mol [21].

Carl Wilhelm Scheele isolated lactic acid from sour milk in 1780; the name comes from the Latin word for milk. Jöns Jacob Berzelius found in 1808 that it is produced in muscle during exertion, Louis Pasteur identified the role of Lactobacillus in its formation in 1856, and Johannes Wislicenus established its structure in 1873. Boehringer Ingelheim used the fermentation route commercially in 1895 [1].

Wikipedia also records that Soviet-bloc countries developed lactobacillus fermentation of molasses because of citric and malic acid shortages, which made lactic acid cheaper than citric acid there [1]. Production grew from about 275,000 tonnes in 2006 to over 1.5 million tonnes by the early 2020s [1].

Poly-L-lactic acid is a biodegradable polyester made from lactic acid that breaks down by hydrolysis; it is used in sutures and implants and, as Sculptra, as an injectable facial filler that is thought to stimulate collagen production through a foreign-body reaction involving macrophages [22]. It is a different product from topical lactic acid and is covered below under clinical studies for completeness.
Lactate, the conjugate base, features in exercise physiology as a metabolite produced by working muscle [1].

Lactic acid is sold as a cosmetic and over-the-counter ingredient and as food additive E270 [1]. Topical lactic acid is not a prominent topic on looksmaxxing forums; where exfoliation comes up in appearance communities it is usually discussed under general skin-care routines, in which Wikipedia reports dermatological consensus prioritizes gentle cleansing, moisturization and sun protection [23].

Human studies of topical lactic acid include a 2014 open trial of 82 percent lactic acid peels in 20 people with melasma at Rohilkhand Medical College, India, every two weeks for 12 weeks with follow-up to 24 weeks [4], a registered comparison of ammonium lactate and urea in xerosis [2], a moisturization study of a lactate lotion with ceramides [3], and the 1999 trial on stinging in rosacea [10].

Separate, related literature concerns poly-L-lactic acid injectables, which are not topical lactic acid. A 2024 systematic review of 11 randomized trials of PLLA in facial aesthetics reported increased dermal thickness and improved lipoatrophy scores in several trials, with effects sustained for at least 25 months [6]. A 2026 systematic review compared PLLA and calcium hydroxyapatite biostimulators [14]. Randomized trials include Sculptra for cheek wrinkles, a Gana V versus Sculptra split-face trial for nasolabial folds, and a midface volume trial [15][16][17]. A registered trial tested immediate versus deferred PLLA injections for HIV facial lipoatrophy and was terminated [18].
